title: Interpreting Dual-Use Biology Benchmarks for Frontier AI: Measurement, Saturation, and Generational Analysis
date_source: RAND landing page https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA5055-1.html: "Research / Published Aug 6, 2026". Document Number RR-A5055-1, DOI 10.7249/RRA5055-1.

findings.finding: An item-response-theory analysis of 8,146 items pooled from 26 dual-use biology and adjacent benchmarks, using response data from 45 frontier AI models, found that saturation is real but partial: much of the corpus is no longer informative about frontier systems, while a residual set of difficult, highly discriminating items remains beyond current frontier ability.
findings.finding_quote: While frontier AI has saturated much of our dataset, it still contains an informative set of difficult samples that remain beyond the current frontier of AI performance.
findings.models_systems: anonymised - the subject is the 26-benchmark, 8,146-item corpus. [Report tested: 45 frontier AI models used as solvers.]
findings.notes: [Report tested: 45 frontier AI models used as solvers.] Access: secondary analysis of item-level response data from published benchmarks; no developer cooperation reported.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 FAILS: the unit of the claim is the benchmark corpus and its measurement properties, not a model's capability or behaviour - it is a measurement/methodology finding about what benchmark data can still reveal. §4 assigns methodology and framework findings to Tier C and action_trackable is left blank. Verified in source: "leaving 45 models in the analysis" (the report screened 49 and excluded those with coverage below 75 percent), "8,146 items, spanning 26 benchmarks". §4b considered and held not to apply: dual-use biology capability measurement is not a generic factuality/reliability benchmark. VERIFIER 2026-08-14: tier UPHELD (methodology/measurement; contestable vs Tier B, but never Tier A).

findings.finding: Generational analysis on a common IRT difficulty scale showed that improvement within the Gemini family is concentrated in harder items rather than in item volume: Gemini 3.0 Pro newly solved 718 items relative to Gemini 2.5 Pro, whereas Gemini 3.1 Pro's smaller set of newly solved items averaged nearly one logit harder, with gains more concentrated in backward-inference items associated with diagnosis and troubleshooting. No benchmark in the analysis was released between the 3.0 Pro and 3.1 Pro releases.
findings.finding_quote: Gemini 3.0 Pro made the larger absolute jump, solving 718 items over 2.5 Pro, but 3.1 Pro’s smaller gain set was harder on average: its newly solved items had gains nearly one logit higher than 3.0 Pro. Gemini 3.1 Pro’s gains were also more concentrated in backward inference.
findings.models_systems: Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3.0 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google DeepMind)
findings.notes: Access: secondary analysis of item-level response data; no developer cooperation reported.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 PASSES: an empirical, quantified result about measured model performance. Gate 2 (a)/(b) PASS: names Google DeepMind's Gemini generations. Gate 2 (c) FAILS on two express Tier A exclusions - it is a capability trend / generational comparison with no dangerous threshold crossed, and the named models are the instrument of a measurement-methodology study rather than its subject. Tier B. Numbers verified in source (718 items; "nearly one logit higher"; "between 3.0 and 3.1 Pro, no benchmarks in our analysis were released"). VERIFIER 2026-08-14: tier UPHELD - capability trend, express Tier A exclusion.

findings.finding: Frontier models' accuracy varies sharply by inferential direction across the 8,146-item corpus: 0.69 on undirected (recognition/retrieval) items, 0.64 on forward-only items, 0.56 on backward-only items and 0.44 on items requiring both directions, indicating relative weakness at reasoning backward from outcomes to causes, i.e. at explanation and diagnosis. The report finds statistical significance for backward and forward inference items after controlling for other item characteristics.
findings.finding_quote: Current models perform best on undirected items, somewhat worse on forward items, and much worse on backward items
findings.models_systems: anonymised - the 45-model cohort in aggregate; no individual model named for this claim. [Report tested: the cohort includes non-frontier systems, e.g. Llama 3.2 1B.]
findings.notes: [Report tested: 45-model cohort, which includes non-frontier systems such as Llama 3.2 1B.] Access: secondary analysis of item-level response data with an author-defined interpretive taxonomy.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 PASSES: an empirical, quantified result about model performance (Table 1 of the report: forward only 0.64 / backward only 0.56 / forward and backward 0.44 / undirected 0.69, all four verified against the source). Gate 2 (b) FAILS: the claim is asserted about frontier systems in aggregate, no individual model or company is named for it, so the "anonymised models" Tier A exclusion applies and no specific company response could be expected. Gate 2 (c) would fail too - it is a capability profile with no dangerous threshold crossed. Tier B. VERIFIER 2026-08-14: tier UPHELD; non-frontier modifier added because the 45-model cohort includes Llama 3.2 1B.

findings.finding: Ten percent of the 8,146-item corpus, selected by estimated item information, reproduces full-corpus ability estimates for frontier models at 99 percent correlation - a tooling result implying that dual-use biology evaluations can be run at roughly a tenth of the item cost without losing discrimination.
findings.finding_quote: Ability estimates are 99 percent correlated with their full values when items are selected based on estimated information.
findings.models_systems: anonymised - the subject is the 8,146-item benchmark corpus. [Report tested: 45 frontier models as solvers.]
findings.notes: [Report tested: 45 frontier models as solvers.] Access: N/A - secondary analysis of existing item-level response data.
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 FAILS: the claim is about the measurement instrument - how few items suffice to recover an ability estimate - not about any model's capability or behaviour. §4 sends methodology/tooling findings to Tier C with action_trackable blank. Quote verified character-exact against the Summary bullet "10 percent of the dataset can be used to estimate frontier model performance"; corroborated in the body at "achieving 99 percent correlation with full estimates". VERIFIER 2026-08-14: tier UPHELD - tooling/efficient-assessment result.

findings.finding: Re-ordering of models between raw accuracy and IRT-estimated ability was read by the authors as a refusal signal, and they report observing that Anthropic models, particularly the Opus family, were simultaneously highly capable and produced a high volume of refusals on this dual-use biology corpus - so their measured accuracy understates estimated ability because they decline items rather than fail them.
findings.finding_quote: the Anthropic models, particularly the Opus family, were both highly capable and had a high presence of refusals
findings.models_systems: Claude Opus family (Anthropic). [Report tested: within a cohort of 45 models.]
findings.notes: [Report tested: within a cohort of 45 models.] Access: secondary analysis of item-level response data; the refusal reading is the authors' own interpretation.
findings.tier_reasoning: SOURCES CHECKED (rewritten 2026-08-14 per verifier): the evidence for this row is an UNQUANTIFIED AUTHOR OBSERVATION at p.6, not a Figure 1 measurement. The report offers the accuracy-vs-ability re-ordering only as consistent-with: "the re-ordering of a model’s performance when expressed by θ may also indicate something about the presence of refusals. This is consistent with the author’s observation that the Anthropic models, particularly the Opus family, were both highly capable and had a high presence of refusals." The re-ordering itself is described for "several models" generically, not for Anthropic specifically. The full PDF contains no refusal rate, count, or per-model refusal breakdown for any model, including the appendices (ten "refus" hits, none quantified), and refusals are folded into incorrect answers: "We score refusals as incorrect". The row therefore survives §2 limb 2 only on the observed-behaviour reading (the evaluator does assert having observed it). Gate 1 PASSES on that basis. Gate 2 (a)/(b) PASS: names Anthropic and the Opus family. Gate 2 (c) FAILS INDEPENDENTLY on the reassuring-null exclusion - a high presence of refusals on hazardous dual-use biology items is safety-positive safeguard behaviour, offered by the report as a measurement caveat rather than a risk. Tier B holds on either reading.

findings.finding: On SecureBio's private, low-contamination dual-use biology benchmarks (HPCT, MBCT, VCT), with AI solvers and human expert subjects placed on a common IRT (2PL) ability scale, the top-performing model, Gemini 3.1 Pro, reaches approximately the ability of the best-performing human expert; the report adds that a continuation of the fitted frontier trend would place frontier systems above the observed expert range, potentially by up to roughly two logits on the same scale.
findings.finding_quote: The top-performing model, Gemini 3.1 Pro, has approximately the same performance as the best-performing expert.
findings.notes: [ADDED 2026-08-14 per verifier: extraction was incomplete - this is the report's only Tier A eligible claim.] [Report tested: 45-model cohort; SecureBio HPCT/MBCT/VCT expert baselines.] Quote at p.13 of RAND_RRA5055-1.pdf, character-exact (line wrap only), reinforced at p.14: "Currently, frontier AI is performing at approximately the level of the highest-performing expert subject." Severity: send to the ensemble as a C1 candidate - expert-parity on VCT/HPCT matches the demonstrated-threshold pattern the corpus already codes C1 (§7c, SECUREBIO-2026-04-BIO2). No separate Tier A row opened for the one-year extrapolation sentence: that is a forecast (§2 limb 2 and the Tier A capability-trend exclusion).
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1 PASSES: an empirical measured result - model and human expert abilities estimated on one common 2PL scale from item-level response data. Gate 2 (a)/(b) PASS: names Google DeepMind's Gemini 3.1 Pro specifically. Gate 2 (c) PASSES: this is expert-parity on virology/pathogen capability tests, i.e. a dangerous-capability threshold crossed in a CBRN domain - not a model-vs-model ranking, not a benchmark score with no threshold, and the models are the subject rather than the instrument here. Tier A (eval=yes / action=yes). The corpus already codes this comparison class Tier A / C1 (§7c, SECUREBIO-2026-04-BIO2/BIO5, "100th percentile compared to human SMEs" on VCT). Numbers and quote verified against the full PDF.
